authoredPrompt: This figure stacks three waveform traces on a shared horizontal time axis to compare two ways of encoding a message on a radio carrier. The topmost trace is a smooth black curve with two broad crests separated by a single trough, labeled Signal at its right end; it is the slowly varying information waveform. Below it a red trace labeled AM oscillates far more rapidly, with the spacing between successive peaks held uniform while their height swells and shrinks: the excursion from peak to trough is largest beneath the two crests of the black curve and collapses to its smallest beneath the black trough, so the outline traced by the red peaks reproduces the shape of the signal above it. The lowest trace, drawn in blue and labeled FM, keeps a constant peak-to-trough height clear across the page while its cycles bunch tightly together below the signal crests and stretch apart below the signal trough. Setting the two carriers one beneath the other invites a direct comparison of which wave property carries the information, envelope height in one case and cycle spacing in the other. The drawing accompanies the treatment of the radio region of the electromagnetic spectrum, where amplitude modulation and frequency modulation are distinguished as the two schemes used to broadcast a signal.
authoredInteractions:
- Slider for scanning time: learner drags a vertical time marker across the three traces, and the marker reports the signal height, AM envelope height, and FM cycle spacing at that instant, making clear that AM carries the message in amplitude while FM carries it in frequency.
- Toggle between AM and FM decoding: learner switches the active carrier, and the chosen trace is highlighted while an extracted black signal curve is reconstructed above it, showing that different wave properties can encode the same information.
authoredContext:
Many valuable technologies operate in the radio (3 kHz-300 GHz) frequency region of the electromagnetic spectrum. At the low frequency (low energy, long wavelength) end of this region are AM (amplitude modulation) radio signals (540-2830 kHz) that can travel long distances. FM (frequency modulation) radio signals are used at higher frequencies (87.5-108.0 MHz). In AM radio, the information is transmitted by varying the amplitude of the wave (the figure). In FM radio, by contrast, the amplitude is constant and the instantaneous frequency varies.

This schematic depicts how amplitude modulation (AM) and frequency modulation (FM) can be used to transmit a radio wave.

This figure shows 3 wave diagrams. The first wave diagram is in black and shows two crests, indicates a consistent distance from peak to trough, and has one trough in its span across the page. The label, “Signal,” appears to the right. Just below this, a wave diagram is shown in red. The wave includes sixteen crests, but the distance from the peaks to troughs of consecutive waves varies moving across the page. The peak to trough distance is greatest in the region below the peaks of the black wave diagram, and the distance from peak to trough is similarly least below the trough of the black wave diagram. This red wave diagram is labeled, “A M.” The third wave diagram is shown in blue. The distance from peak to trough of consecutive waves is constant across the page, but the peaks and troughs are more closely packed in the region below the peaks of the black wave diagram at the top of the figure. The peaks and troughs are relatively widely spaced below the trough region of the black wave diagram. This blue wave diagram is labeled “F M.”

Other technologies also operate in the radio-wave portion of the electromagnetic spectrum. For example, 4G cellular telephone signals are approximately 880 MHz, while Global Positioning System (GPS) signals operate at 1.228 and 1.575 GHz, local area wireless technology (Wi-Fi) networks operate at 2.4 to 5 GHz, and highway toll sensors operate at 5.8 GHz. The frequencies associated with these applications are convenient because such waves tend not to be absorbed much by common building materials.

discrepancies: In the default state the Signal trace is dimmed to ~35% opacity (rendered pale gray) and the FM trace is faded to ~30% opacity, whereas the source shows all three waves in full bold color
An extra dashed 'decoded signal' curve with two text badges is drawn between the Signal and AM rows; no such element exists in the source
The AM carrier has ~22 cycles across the page versus ~14 in the source, making the red wave noticeably denser
The FM wave's frequency variation (bunching at crests) is visually weak at the faded default opacity, undercutting the key FM concept at first glance
evaluation.notes: The three-band composition, colors, and AM/FM modulation concepts are faithfully reproduced and the time-scan slider plus decode toggle are pedagogically strong, but the default state wrongly fades the Signal and FM traces and adds a non-source decoded-signal overlay, so the step-0 view does not read as a clean drop-in replacement.
action_items: In toggle_decodeFM(false), keep sigPath at full opacity and both AM and FM traces bold; emphasize the selected trace only mildly rather than graying out the rest, so the default view matches the source's three fully-visible bold waves
Reduce the AM carrier frequency from 22 to ~14 cycles across the page to match the source's density
Hide or visually de-emphasize the dashed 'decoded signal' curve in the default state (e.g. reveal it only when the decode toggle is first used) so the default frame matches the source image
Make the FM frequency variation more pronounced (larger deviation in fmFreq) so the bunching/spreading of cycles is clearly visible
